sources.title: Euler's identity - Wikipedia
sources.excerpt: Euler's identity is the equality e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0, connecting five fundamental mathematical constants.

sources.title: Exponential function - Wikipedia
sources.excerpt: The exponential function can be extended to complex arguments and is connected with sine and cosine through Euler's formula.

sources.title: Taylor series - Wikipedia
sources.excerpt: A Taylor series represents a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from its derivatives at one point.

ai_module.summary: A bridge between exponential growth and circular motion in the complex plane.
ai_module.explanation: The formula writes a complex exponential in terms of cosine and sine. It is commonly used as a prerequisite when interpreting Euler's identity at x = pi.

ai_module.summary: A local power-series representation built from a function's derivatives.
ai_module.explanation: Taylor series provide one standard route for defining and analyzing exponential and trigonometric functions as infinite series.

ai_module.summary: A compact identity connecting five fundamental mathematical constants.
ai_module.explanation: Euler's identity follows by evaluating Euler's formula at x = pi. Its compact form links the complex exponential with the additive and multiplicative identities.
derivation_steps: Use cos(pi) = -1 and sin(pi) = 0 to obtain e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0.

user_module.notes: Compare the identity with the unit-circle interpretation.

edges.rationale: Evaluating the complex exponential formula at x = pi produces Euler's identity.
Series definitions of the exponential and trigonometric functions provide a derivation basis for Euler's formula and its special case.
